passage:
'You want to know why I still go to the temple with Paati? Okay. Last year I was reading all these articles and had a hundred questions. Like, if God is everywhere, why the temple? Why the rules about who can enter? I was scared to ask anyone at home. I thought they'd say college had spoiled me.
Finally I blurted it out to Minakshi Paati while we were stringing jasmine. She didn't even drop the thread. She said, "Good, Sharmila. Our sages argued about exactly that for a thousand years. Asking is old, kanna. Only the fear is new."
Then she asked what I thought. Actually asked. We argued till the flowers wilted.
I still have questions. But I go with her on Fridays. Because she let me ask.'

qa.q: What were Sharmila and Minakshi Paati doing when the question came out?
qa.a: They were stringing jasmine.

qa.q: Why was Sharmila scared to ask anyone at home?
qa.a: Sharmila feared being told that college had spoiled things, so the questions felt shameful to voice.

qa.q: What did Minakshi Paati do that kept Sharmila close?
qa.a: She welcomed the question, said the sages argued about the same thing, used no shame or fear, and asked what Sharmila thought.

qa.q: How might Minakshi Paati feel arguing with her grandchild till the flowers wilted?
qa.a: She probably enjoys it and feels closer, seeing curiosity as part of faith rather than a threat to it.

grounding: It shows an elder meeting a young person's doubts with interest and no shame, which keeps both the relationship and the temple visits alive.

I only saw it because I'd gone to the temple near our hostel for the prasad, honestly. Santosh, my roommate, had been quiet for weeks; there was a book on evolution and a copy of the Gita on his desk, both full of sticky notes.
After the evening aarti he walked up to the old priest and asked something. I couldn't hear most of it, only 'but how can both be true?' His ears were red. I thought he might get scolded.
The priest laughed, not at him, and patted the step beside him. They sat there for maybe forty minutes. The priest did most of the listening. At one point he said, loud enough for me to hear, 'Arjuna had doubts too, in the middle of a battlefield.'
Walking back, Santosh didn't say much. But he was humming.

qa.q: What two books were on Santosh's desk?
qa.a: A book on evolution and a copy of the Gita, both full of sticky notes.

qa.q: What might Santosh's red ears suggest as he asks the priest?
qa.a: They suggest he was nervous and perhaps embarrassed, unsure whether asking would bring a scolding.

qa.q: How did the priest's response help, going by what the narrator saw?
qa.a: He laughed kindly, invited Santosh to sit, mostly listened, and pointed out that Arjuna had doubts too, treating questions as normal.

qa.q: How does the narrator read Santosh's humming on the walk back?
qa.a: The narrator can't be sure, but takes it as a sign that Santosh felt lighter after being heard.

grounding: It shows, through a roommate's eyes, a priest welcoming a young man's doubts with interest and reminding him that doubt is old and common.

First week. At the Sunday study circle in the ashram library, Ira finally asked the question she had carried for months: "If God is good, why did my friend's baby brother die?" The room went silent. She waited to be scolded.
Jatin, who led the circle, only leaned forward. "That's one of the oldest questions people have ever asked. Saints asked it. Tell me more about what you've been thinking."
Third week. Ira brought a list. Why pray if everything is already decided? Why do different scriptures say different things? Jatin didn't have neat answers to all of them. For some he said, "I don't know. Here's what I've read. Here's what others think."
Sixth week. Ira noticed she no longer felt guilty for asking. She still came every Sunday. When her mother asked whether she still believed, Ira said, "I'm not sure. But I'm still in the conversation."

qa.q: What question did Ira ask in the first week?
qa.a: If God is good, why did my friend's baby brother die?

qa.q: What did Ira feel waiting after her first question?
qa.a: She felt anxious and braced to be scolded or shamed for asking.

qa.q: Why did Jatin's response keep Ira coming back?
qa.a: He met her questions with interest, called them old and common, admitted when he didn't know, and never used shame or fear.

qa.q: What might Jatin feel leading these conversations?
qa.a: Jatin likely feels respect and interest, valuing honest questions even without neat answers.

grounding: Over weeks a study-circle leader meets a young woman's questions with interest and without shame, keeping her in the conversation.

Aditi, you're afraid to tell your parents about your questions. Let me tell you about Lalremsiami at nineteen, in Aizawl.
I sang in the church choir every Sunday. Then I read a book from the college library about the world's religions, and the questions poured out: why so many faiths, if only one is true? Why would a loving God turn anyone away? I was terrified. I thought asking was itself a sin.
One evening after choir I stayed back and asked old Pastor Zothan. My voice shook. He smiled and said, "Child, the Psalms are full of people shouting questions at God. You're in good company." He didn't threaten me with fear or shame. He gave me books by believers and by doubters and said, "Come back and argue with me."
I argued with him for three years. I stayed in the church, but by choice now, not by fear. That old man gave me permission to think. So ask your questions.

qa.q: What did young Lalremsiami read that started the questions?
qa.a: A book from the college library about the world's religions.

qa.q: What did young Lalremsiami feel before asking the pastor?
qa.a: Lalremsiami felt terrified, believing that even asking might be a sin.

qa.q: What turning point came when young Lalremsiami asked Pastor Zothan?
qa.a: He welcomed the questions, said doubt is old and common, and gave books from both sides instead of using shame, which kept Lalremsiami in the conversation.

qa.q: How might Pastor Zothan have seen the young choir singer's questions?
qa.a: He likely saw them as a sign of thoughtful faith and felt fond and patient, inviting more argument.

grounding: An elder recalls how a pastor met her youthful questions with interest, not fear or shame, which kept both the relationship and her faith.

On the night before Gurpurab the power went out in their lane in Amritsar, and the langar preparation moved to candlelight in the courtyard. Gurleen and her college friend Imran were chopping onions beside her Biji when the question she had been swallowing for weeks slipped out.
"Biji, what if the Gurus were just wise men? What if the stories aren't literally true?"
Her mother, stirring the dal, froze. Imran stopped chopping.
Biji didn't. She kept kneading, then laughed softly. "You think you're the first to ask that? Guru Nanak himself asked questions wherever he went. Asking is not a sin, puttar. Being afraid to ask is worse."
She told Gurleen about her own doubts as a young bride, and the granthi who had listened instead of scolding. "Come with me to the gurdwara tomorrow. Ask Bhai-ji too. He likes a good question."
In the flickering light, Gurleen felt something unknot in her chest. Imran grinned and went back to the onions.

qa.q: Where did the langar preparation move during the power cut?
qa.a: To candlelight in the courtyard.

qa.q: What did Gurleen feel when her Biji laughed?
qa.a: She felt relieved and lighter, the fear of asking unknotting in her chest.

qa.q: What did Biji do that kept Gurleen close to the faith?
qa.a: She welcomed the question with interest, said doubt is old and common, shared her own doubts, and invited Gurleen to ask the granthi.

qa.q: What might Gurleen's mother have felt when she froze?
qa.a: Her mother probably felt alarmed and worried, until Biji's calm response eased the moment.

grounding: In a power cut, a grandmother meets a young woman's first doubts with interest, calling them old and common and using no shame or fear.

passage: Lalit had been dreading the Sunday lunch at Usha Bua's flat in Pune ever since he'd posted a question online: "Why would a kind God allow floods?" His cousins had forwarded it to the family group. Bua, who did her prayers at five every morning, served him extra rice and then sat down beside him. "So. The flood question." Lalit braced himself. "It's a good one," she said. "People have asked it for thousands of years. There are whole books on it, some from our own tradition. Asking doesn't make you a bad person, beta." She went to her shelf and brought back a worn book with her notes in the margins. "I argued with this one at your age. Read it, and tell me where you disagree." Lalit laughed, surprised. The tight knot in his stomach loosened. He stayed until evening, talking.

qa.q: What did Usha Bua bring back from her shelf?
qa.a: She brought back a worn book with her notes in the margins.

qa.q: How did Lalit feel before and after Bua called his question a good one?
qa.a: Lalit felt anxious and braced for a scolding at first, then relieved and surprised when the knot in his stomach loosened.

qa.q: Which of Bua's choices kept Lalit close?
qa.a: She met the question with interest, said doubt is old and common, used no shame, and invited him to read and disagree, so he felt safe to keep talking.

qa.q: What would have changed if Bua had scolded Lalit in front of the family?
qa.a: Lalit would likely have felt ashamed and kept his questions hidden, drifting away from both Bua and the faith.

grounding: Shows an elder meeting a young person's questions with interest, calling doubt old and common and using no shame or fear.
